title: Assign Kubernetes Services to DLP Group Rules
summary: Use the mock-lab orders demo to preview a DLP group rule change, spot extra Kubernetes workloads, and verify masking on fresh captures.
body_markdown:
You want to mask the` customer` field in captured checkout traffic. The payments team already has a DLP group rule that masks that field, so you open **Add to DLP rule** on the checkout service. The preview shows one more workload. The orders service running next to checkout would also start masking` customer` .


You can reproduce that decision with the orders app in[mock-lab’s Kubernetes tutorial](https://github.com/speedscale/mock-lab/tree/main/tutorial/k8s) . You’ll run the same app in three workload locations, see why the rule would expand, then save a scoped copy and check fresh captures from all three.[Watch the Feature Spotlight](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/XtO4l7GXvsU)


## 1. Deploy the mock-lab orders demo


Use a dedicated test Speedscale account and Kubernetes cluster. You’ll need Git,` kubectl` , permission to create namespaces and deployments, and admin access to the Speedscale dashboard. The cluster should already have a connected Speedscale forwarder with **Redact sensitive data** on and the standard operator configured for eBPF capture in both exercise namespaces. The demo pulls published container images and the orders app calls the hosted demo catalog.[Install the Kubernetes operator](https://docs.speedscale.com/getting-started/installation/install/kubernetes/) ·[Configure eBPF capture](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/capture/kubernetes/) ·[Configure the forwarder baseline](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/dlp/applying-rules/)


Start a Bash shell. Replace` speedscale-dlp-test` with your test kubeconfig context and check the displayed cluster before applying anything. Use a test cluster where` dlp-payments` and` dlp-shop` are available for this exercise. Run the rest of the terminal commands from the mock-lab repository root in that shell.


```text
export   DLP_CONTEXT  =  'speedscale-dlp-test'
kubectl   config   get-contexts   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "


git   clone   https://github.com/speedscale/mock-lab.git
cd   mock-lab


for   namespace   in   dlp-payments   dlp-shop  ;   do
kubectl   kustomize   tutorial/k8s/overlays/go   |
sed   -e   "s/^  name: tutorial$/  name:   $namespace  /"   \
-e   "s/^  namespace: tutorial$/  namespace:   $namespace  /"   |
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   apply   -f   -
done


sed   -e   's/tutorial-orders/checkout/g'   \
-e   's#image: checkout#image: ghcr.io/speedscale/mock-lab-tutorial-go:latest#'   \
tutorial/k8s/base/app.yaml   |
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   -n   dlp-shop   apply   -f   -


kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   -n   dlp-payments   rollout   status   deploy/tutorial-orders   --timeout=4m
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   -n   dlp-shop   rollout   status   deploy/tutorial-orders   --timeout=4m
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   -n   dlp-shop   rollout   status   deploy/checkout   --timeout=4m
```


The overlay creates an orders deployment and Postgres in each namespace. The last apply reuses the same app as` checkout` and points it at the Postgres service already running in` dlp-shop` . Renaming the deployment, its Service, selector, and pod` app` label gives Speedscale a distinct service to assign. These are the three workloads you’ll compare.


Namespace Pod` app` label Role in the exercise


` dlp-payments`` tutorial-orders` Already covered by the payments rule


` dlp-shop`` checkout` The service you want to add


` dlp-shop`` tutorial-orders` The extra workload the preview will find


LLM prompt for this step


```text
Read the mock-lab tutorial/k8s README and this article's deployment commands. Use only my approved test kubeconfig context <test-context> and test Speedscale account. Show the context and cluster before applying anything. Ensure the dlp-payments and dlp-shop namespace names are free. From the mock-lab root, render and deploy the Go tutorial overlay in both namespaces. Reuse the app manifest to deploy checkout in dlp-shop with its own app label and Service. Verify all three app rollouts and report the namespace and app label for each. Leave the context and clone location available for the following steps.
```


## 2. Capture the synthetic orders


Enable eBPF capture for the three app deployments. Speedscale uses the deployment annotation to attach capture to the workloads. In this setup the jobs send HTTP requests from inside the cluster to the three Services.


```text
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   -n   dlp-payments   annotate   deploy/tutorial-orders   \
capture.speedscale.com/enabled=  true   --overwrite
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   -n   dlp-shop   annotate   deploy/tutorial-orders   deploy/checkout   \
capture.speedscale.com/enabled=  true   --overwrite


send_orders  () {
local   namespace  =  "  $1  "   service  =  "  $2  "   job
job  =  $(
sed   -e   "s/^  namespace: tutorial$/  namespace:   $namespace  /"   \
-e   "s/tutorial-orders/  $service  /g"   tutorial/k8s/traffic/job.yaml   |
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   create   -f   -   -o   name
)   ||   return
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   -n   "  $namespace  "   \
wait   --for=condition=complete   "  $job  "   --timeout=5m   &&
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   -n   "  $namespace  "   logs   "  $job  "   -c   traffic
}


send_orders   dlp-payments   tutorial-orders
send_orders   dlp-shop   tutorial-orders
send_orders   dlp-shop   checkout
```


Each Job should log` sent 135 requests, 0 unexpected` . That confirms the requests made it through. Check capture separately in **Infrastructure** and **Traffic** in Speedscale. Find the three locations and open a fresh inbound` POST /orders` request from each. The synthetic` customer` value, such as` ada@example.com` , should be visible in the captured request body before you add the lab rule. If an existing policy already masks that field, use a clean test account for this comparison.


LLM prompt for this step


```text
In the same mock-lab clone and approved test context, annotate the three app deployments for eBPF capture and run the article's send_orders function once per workload. Report each Job's completion status and traffic count. In the approved Speedscale dashboard, check for a fresh inbound POST /orders per workload and confirm the synthetic customer field is visible before the lab rule. Keep the DLP_CONTEXT value and send_orders function for the post-save run. Report any missing capture or existing mask before proceeding.
```


## 3. Create the starting DLP group rule


In **DLP Rules** , create` dlp-lab-payments` . Under **Scope** , select **Group rule** , enter` Payments` as the **Owner** , and set **Clusters** to your test cluster’s name as displayed in Speedscale. Set **Namespaces** to` dlp-payments` and **Services** to` tutorial-orders` . Under **Mask fields by name** , enter` customer` in **Field or header name** and click **Add** . Turn on **Enabled** in **Scope** , then save. Leave the cluster’s **Redaction rule** setting in **Infrastructure** unchanged. The group rule applies when the workload matches its scope.[Dashboard rule setup](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/dlp/group-rules-dashboard/#create-a-group-rule) ·[Masking by field name](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/dlp/creating-rules/#masking-fields-by-name)


A rule save reloads the forwarders connected to the account and can pause capture briefly. Wait for the test cluster’s forwarder to come back before generating traffic for verification. The **DLP rules** section on the service page shows the baseline and any matching group rules for each location. On` checkout` , the payments rule should be absent at this point.[How saved rules take effect](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/dlp/group-rules-dashboard/#when-a-saved-rule-takes-effect)


## 4. Check what else the scope would cover


Open **Services** , select **checkout** , and click **Add to DLP rule** in the **DLP rules** section. Under **Where** , keep the test cluster and` dlp-shop` selected. Under **Rule** , choose` dlp-lab-payments` .


The preview shows` + dlp-shop` under **Namespaces** and` + checkout` under **Services** . Under **Also masks** , look for` tutorial-orders` in` dlp-shop` . The rule checks each list independently. One listed namespace and one listed service must match, so adding` dlp-shop` gives every service already listed another place to match. If` checkout` later starts running in` dlp-payments` , the widened rule would match it there too.


Save choice` dlp-payments / tutorial-orders`` dlp-shop / checkout`` dlp-shop / tutorial-orders`


Add to` dlp-lab-payments` Original rule Original rule Original rule


Create a copy for` checkout` Original rule Scoped copy Baseline only


**Add to dlp-lab-payments** is selected by default. For this exercise, select **Create a copy that covers only checkout** , leave the copy name as` dlp-lab-payments-checkout` , and create it. The copy carries over the masking and owner, with the scope set to the selected checkout location. If the preview says a location could not be checked, resolve that before choosing to widen the original.[How group-rule scope matches workloads](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/dlp/group-rules/)


## 5. Verify masking on fresh captures


Confirm the copy appears under **DLP rules** on` checkout` and the original rule still covers` dlp-payments / tutorial-orders` . After the forwarder comes back, rerun the traffic jobs from the same Bash shell.


```text
send_orders   dlp-payments   tutorial-orders
send_orders   dlp-shop   checkout
send_orders   dlp-shop   tutorial-orders
```


In **Traffic** , select a time range after the save. Filter to an inbound` POST /orders` from each workload and compare its captured request body. Look for a` REDACTED-` token in` customer` for` checkout` and` dlp-payments / tutorial-orders` . The same field in` dlp-shop / tutorial-orders` should still contain the synthetic value. Comparing a newly masked request with a fresh out-of-scope request tells you more than the rule’s saved settings alone.[Inspect captured request bodies](https://docs.speedscale.com/guides/capture/bodies/)


LLM prompt for the scope and verification steps


```text
Use my approved test Speedscale dashboard and the three mock-lab workloads. Follow the article to create the enabled dlp-lab-payments group rule with owner Payments, the test cluster, namespace dlp-payments, service tutorial-orders, and the customer mask. From checkout, choose Add to DLP rule and report the two added scope values and the exact workload under Also masks. Choose the scoped copy for checkout and verify both saved scopes. When the forwarder is back, use the existing send_orders function in the mock-lab root for all three workloads. Inspect recent inbound POST /orders captures and report which customer values were masked and whether the out-of-scope order remained visible. Keep all changes in the test account and report any unavailable check.
```


## Clean up the lab


In the test dashboard, turn off both lab rules and save before deleting them. Disabling delivers the change to the forwarder. Deleting alone does not trigger a reload. Remove the two namespaces you created after you finish reviewing the captures.


```text
kubectl   --context   "  $DLP_CONTEXT  "   delete   namespace   dlp-payments   dlp-shop
```


LLM prompt for cleanup


```text
Clean up this exercise in the same approved test account and Kubernetes context. Disable and save only dlp-lab-payments and dlp-lab-payments-checkout before deleting them. Confirm dlp-payments and dlp-shop are the namespaces created for this run, remove them, and report what was removed or remains.
```


For your next scope change, start from a service and use **Also masks** to decide whether to extend the existing policy or save a copy. If you need to design the baseline and group rules first, start with[Team-Based DLP](https://speedscale.com/blog/team-based-dlp-group-rules/) and see how those rules affect[traffic replay and testing](https://speedscale.com/blog/dlp-traffic-replay-and-the-missing-link-to-software-quality/) .


## Frequently asked questions


### Why does adding one service to a DLP group rule sometimes mask another workload?


The rule matches one value in each of its cluster, namespace, and service lists. Adding a namespace gives the services already listed another place to match. Also masks shows the extra running workloads the dashboard finds.


### Does copying a DLP group rule change the original?


The copy keeps the owner's name and the original rule's masking settings at the time of the copy. It has its own scope and can be edited independently. The original keeps its existing scope.


### Do I need admin access to assign a service?


Yes. Speedscale admins can use Add to DLP rule and save the change. Other signed-in users can view the rules that match a service.


### Can I verify a rule change against traffic captured earlier?


Use traffic captured after the forwarder reloads. The earlier capture reflects the rule configuration in effect when it was recorded.
